title: The Story of Mexico's Dia de los Muertos
paragraphs: Every year at the beginning of November, families across Mexico celebrate Día de los Muertos, or the Day of the Dead. Despite its name, the holiday is not a sad occasion. Instead, it is a colorful celebration in which people remember and honor loved ones who have died.
The holiday is generally celebrated on November 1 and 2. According to tradition, these are the days when the spirits of the dead return to visit their families.

The origins of Día de los Muertos are complex. Many accounts trace the holiday to the cultures of ancient Mesoamerica, the region that includes present-day Mexico and Central America. The Aztecs, for instance, held festivals to honor the dead, and some sources connect the holiday to Mictecacihuatl, the Aztec goddess of the dead. However, not all historians agree with this explanation. Some argue that the holiday was largely introduced by the Spanish, who brought the Catholic observances of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day to Mexico after they conquered the Aztec Empire in 1521. Today, most sources describe the celebration as a blend of Indigenous and Catholic traditions.

At the heart of the holiday is the ofrenda, an altar that families build in their homes. Ofrendas typically include photographs of the people who have died, as well as their favorite foods and drinks. They are often decorated with candles and bright orange marigold flowers. Many families also visit cemeteries to clean and decorate the graves of their relatives.

Another well-known symbol of the holiday is the skull, or calavera. Decorated sugar skulls are a popular treat, and people often paint their faces to look like skulls. One of the most famous images is La Catrina, an elegant female skeleton wearing a large hat, which was created by the Mexican artist José Guadalupe Posada in the early 20th century.
In 2008, UNESCO added the tradition, under the name "Indigenous Festivity Dedicated to the Dead," to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Today, Día de los Muertos is celebrated not only in Mexico but also by Mexican communities around the world, and its imagery has become familiar to people of many backgrounds.
